slides.script:
Good morning, everyone. My name is Chris Wu, and today I'm presenting my thesis: 'Physical-World Observation for Personal AI Agent Personalization.' [Pause]

Before we dive in, I want you to imagine a scenario. Imagine you have a personal biographer who knows everything about you — your schedule, your emails, your preferences.

But here's the catch: this biographer has never actually met you. They know you bought a book through amazon order history — so they've already decided you're a bookworm. But they didn't see you place it on a high shelf where it's remained untouched.

This gap — between your digital traces and your lived experience — is what my research is about.

slides.subtitle: The Claw
slides.script: First, let me explain several concepts.

slides.subtitle: Personal AI Agents are Here
slides.script:
We're moving from AI assistants to AI agents.

On the left is the traditional AI assistant — reactive, session-based, focused on a single task. Every conversation starts from scratch.

On the right is the personal AI agent — proactive, continuous, with a persistent memory. It doesn't just answer questions. It knows your work, your patterns, your goals. It never forgets who you are.

This is a fundamentally different kind of relationship.

slides.subtitle: The OpenClaw Fever
slides.script:
OpenClaw is at the center of this shift. And the scale of its adoption is remarkable.

From Shenzhen to New York, thousands of people are gathering just to learn how to run this new kind of intelligence on their own machines. It's what I call the 'OpenClaw fever.'

slides.subtitle: What is OpenClaw
slides.script:
So, what exactly is OpenClaw?

Think of it as the operating system for your AI agent. While models like Claude or GPT provide the brain, OpenClaw manages everything around it — your memory, your tasks, your computer environment — locally, on your own machine.

It's the persistent layer that lets an AI act on your behalf and remember you, session after session. The glue that makes the agent feel personal.

slides.subtitle: OpenClaw's Spreading
slides.script:
The deployment map speaks for itself.

Within months, OpenClaw spread to every continent — with dense clusters exceeding 50,000 active instances in both China and the US alone. This wasn't a gradual rollout. It blanketed the planet.

slides.subtitle: OpenClaw's GitHub Stars Growth
slides.script: The data confirms the momentum. OpenClaw reached 100,000 GitHub stars in under a month — overtaking projects like React that took years to reach the same milestone. Whatever your benchmark for rapid growth, this exceeds it.

slides.subtitle: Personalization
slides.script:
But first — what do we actually mean by personalization?

In 2000, Blom defined it as changing a system to increase its personal relevance to the individual. My framing is simpler: the service fits — or better yet, exceeds — your expectations.

Think of it as a spectrum. At one end, systems that barely notice you exist. At the other, human conversation — where every word, every pause, is continuous personalization. That's the level of understanding we're aiming for.

slides.subtitle: Why Personalization Matters
slides.script:
So why does this matter so much for an agent specifically?

Look at the left side. A generic agent doesn't know you. Every task passes through the same fixed bottleneck — your context, your preferences, your goals all get flattened. The output might be technically correct, but it rarely hits what you actually need.

Now look at the right. A personalized agent fuses your history, your preferences, and your workflows into one continuous context. The same task comes in — and it reaches the intended outcome, every time.

This is what I mean when I say: personalization is effectiveness. It's not a nice-to-have. It's the difference between an agent that works and one that doesn't.

slides.subtitle: The Blind Spot
slides.script:
But here's the problem. There is a massive blind spot.

All of that personalization — all of that memory and context — is built entirely from your digital life. What the agent knows about you is limited to what happens on a screen.

The rest of your life is invisible to it.

slides.subtitle: Two Worlds
slides.script:
This blind spot exists because we inhabit two worlds simultaneously.

On the left is the Digital Dimension — the realm of browser tabs, calendar invites, and chat logs that our agents know perfectly.

But on the right is the Physical World — where our actual lives unfold. This is where an agent could finally see that you've been staring at the same paragraph for twenty minutes, or notice the coat still on your chair that means you haven't left the house all day.

Right now, our agents are personalizing from only half the picture.

slides.subtitle: Research Landscape
slides.script:
The idea of recording your life and retrieving it later isn't new.

Vannevar Bush imagined the Memex in 1945 — a machine that could store and link everything you read using microcamera. Gordon Bell spent a decade photographing his every waking moment with MyLifeBits. These projects were as if prophesying the computer and big data era.

Today, as machines learn to "understand" semantics and images, does continuous recording of life enable an agent to better understand you? That's the gap this research addresses.

slides.subtitle: Research Questions
slides.script:
Three research questions, three contributions.

RQ1: What physical-world information becomes visible through egocentric perception that digital traces alone can't capture?

RQ2: In what task and interaction contexts does this information meaningfully improve personalization — and when does it introduce noise or redundancy?

RQ3: What design requirements emerge for integrating continuous egocentric sensing into an existing agent memory architecture?

I'll walk through the system and the study that answer each one.

slides.subtitle: Design Rationale
slides.script: Before I get into the system itself, I want to explain a few key design decisions — choices that shaped everything else.

slides.subtitle: Why Egocentric Vision?
slides.script:
The most fundamental choice was to use egocentric vision — a first-person wearable camera.

The reason is simple: your field of view is already a map of your attention. Whatever you're looking at is, by definition, what you're engaging with. No external sensor can tell you that.

And unlike a fixed camera on the wall, a wearable goes everywhere you do — every room, every environment, every transition. A single frame captures your surroundings, your activity, and the objects around you all at once.

Timing also matters. People built some gigantic egocentric database. Vision-language models have only recently become reliable enough to extract structured meaning from these images.

slides.subtitle: Why OpenClaw?
slides.script:
The second major decision was to build on top of OpenClaw rather than a custom agent.

The key insight is this: OpenClaw personalizes using plain text files — markdown documents that describe who you are, what you're working on, what you prefer. Every session, the agent reads those files before it does anything else.

That means we can inject physical-world observations directly into the agent's memory — without touching its core architecture. We're not hacking the system. We're speaking its language.

And because the memory is plain text, it's fully inspectable. We can trace exactly how a physical observation enters the agent's reasoning.

slides.subtitle: How OpenClaw works
slides.script:
Here's how that actually works. At the start of every session, OpenClaw assembles a 'context window' from these markdown files — your persona, your preferences, your recent logs. The LLM reads all of this before the conversation even begins.

What matters here is that this memory is plain text. You can open it, read it, and edit it yourself. It's not a black box — it's a transparent, human-readable record that grows with every session.

This is exactly the property we're going to take advantage of.

slides.subtitle: System Design
slides.script:
Now let's look at how this actually works. How do we take raw video from a wearable camera and turn it into the kind of knowledge that makes an agent feel personal?

Here's the pipeline.

slides.subtitle: Abstract Pipeline
slides.script:
This is the big picture: a continuous loop moving from Collection, to Compression, then to Integration, and finally Feedback.

I want to pause on Compression — because it is the strategic heart of this entire project.

The physical world generates an overwhelming amount of data. If we tried to record and process every single second, the system would drown. So the question isn't 'how do we capture everything?' The question is: 'how do we decide what matters?'

In this pipeline, to compress is to understand.

Much like the human brain, the system doesn't try to remember every frame. It filters noise to identify key events — moments that actually change something about who you are. By combining AI reasoning with your own feedback, we turn thousands of raw images into a handful of meaningful insights.

Only through this strategic compression can an agent truly understand who you are — not just what you did.

slides.subtitle: The Pipeline & Data Flow
slides.script:
This is the five-layer pipeline that makes the system work.

Notice the boundary in the middle. The first two layers — Capture and Preprocessing — run entirely on the 'edge,' meaning your phone. This keeps the system responsive and handles privacy locally, on your body.

The data then travels to your computer, where the Inference and Memory layers do the heavy lifting — turning filtered snapshots into structured knowledge. Finally, the Retrieval layer connects everything back to the agent, so it can actually use what it has learned.

Think of it like a journalist and an editor working together: one gathers everything in the field, the other decides what's worth publishing. This division of labor is what makes the system powerful enough to think deeply, and light enough to run on a single battery all day.

slides.subtitle: Layer 1 Capture & Layer 1.5 Preprocess
slides.script:
The first design challenge: how do you capture a human life without recording everything?

The answer is adaptive capture. Instead of filming at a fixed interval, the system listens. It monitors ambient sound, movement, and scene changes — signals that something in your environment is shifting. When those signals appear, the camera wakes up and starts capturing.

This means: if you're working quietly at your desk for thirty minutes, barely anything is recorded. But the moment you stand up, move to another room, or start a conversation, the system activates.

The Preprocessing layer then acts as a second filter — automatically scoring each frame for clarity and uniqueness, discarding the blurry or redundant ones.

Together, these two layers define the rhythm of the system: mostly quiet, selectively attentive.

slides.subtitle: Capture Monitor
slides.script: To tune and monitor all of this, I built a monitor page streaming the camera from my phone — so I could observe the system's behavior, adjust the parameters, and verify it was running as intended.

slides.subtitle: Layer 2 Inference
slides.script:
Once we have those snapshots, the Inference layer acts as an intelligent interpreter. It doesn't just see a picture of a room — it looks for meaning.

If you're sitting at your kitchen table with a laptop and a half-eaten sandwich, it doesn't list the objects. It understands the context: this person is probably having a working lunch. It asks — what are they doing, what objects are around them, where are they, and most importantly, why does this moment matter?

One important design detail: each inference pass carries forward the output of the previous batch as part of its input. This means the system always has a sense of what just happened — maintaining continuity across time, not just isolated snapshots.

The output is a structured observation: a readable note that the agent can directly use.

slides.subtitle: Layer 3 Memory
slides.script:
Now let's look at how we organize this knowledge. I designed a four-layer memory architecture — one that mirrors how we naturally process our own experience.

Logs are the base layer. Every raw observation from the camera lands here — like your immediate sensory memory. Unfiltered, granular, complete.

Insights sit above that. Throughout the day, the system reviews the logs and distills them into a snapshot: what's happening right now, what are the key moments so far. Like keeping a running mental note.

Narrative is the nightly reflection. At the end of the day, those moments are woven into a single, coherent timeline.

And Patterns are the long view. Over weeks and months, the system identifies recurring habits and stores them in your behavioral profile.

Here's what makes this different from ordinary memory: it can be corrected. If the system misreads a scene, you can open the file, edit it, and teach it what actually happened. It's a memory you can audit.

slides.subtitle: Server Monitor
slides.script:
I also built a dashboard. Here, you can watch the system's interpretation process in real time.

In the center is the batch feed — raw snapshots coming in, immediately translated into structured observations. The system identifies what's on my desk, what I'm focused on, the context of the moment.

On the right, the memory state shows the agent's running journal — merging those observations into a high-level summary, tracking my current state and daily highlights as they accumulate.

What you're watching is an agent that is no longer operating on guesswork — it is actively witnessing and making sense of my life.

slides.subtitle: Layer 3.5 Retrieval
slides.script:
Finally, we have the Retrieval layer — this is where stored knowledge becomes active assistance.

It works in three ways. The first is Bootstrap: every session begins with the agent already up to speed on your recent context — no need to catch it up.

The second is On-Demand: if you ask something like 'where did I leave that book I was reading?' the agent searches its physical logs and answers from observation, not assumption.

The third is Proactive: the agent can notice something has changed in your physical environment and initiate a conversation on its own.

This is the final step of the loop — turning memory into action.

slides.subtitle: Full Pipeline Overview
slides.script:
Taken together, this pipeline builds a continuous, structured record of a person's physical life — and connects it directly to the agent that works for them.

From the wearable on your body to the memory file in your agent — every layer serves one purpose: closing the gap between the life you live and the AI that's supposed to know you.

slides.subtitle: Study Design
slides.script: To evaluate this system, I ran a two-week autoethnographic study — using a 'research through design' methodology. In plain terms: I was both the designer and the subject.

slides.subtitle: Study Design
slides.script:
The study ran in two phases.

The first was a Calibration phase — where I tuned the pipeline parameters, tested the capture triggers, and adjusted the inference prompts based on real-world performance.

The second was a formal Observation phase. Once everything was set, I froze all system parameters and simply lived with it — letting the system run without intervention, so the data would be clean.

slides.subtitle: Data Collection
slides.script:
Over two weeks, the system collected thousands of egocentric keyframes, full transcripts of every interaction I had with the agent, and daily journal entries where I reflected on what the system got right — and what it got wrong.

These three streams of data — visual, conversational, and interpretive — give a picture that no single method alone could provide.

slides.subtitle: Experimental Protocol
slides.script:
The study used three observation modes.

Passive observation: I went about my day normally, letting the system capture whatever it would.

Structured probes: at specific moments, I asked the agent to recall something from earlier — testing whether the memory was accurate and useful.

And proactive triggers: a scheduled job allowed the agent to initiate contact on its own, based on what it had observed — without me asking.

slides.subtitle: Study Device
slides.script: The capture device was a head-mounted iPhone — an approximation of the smart glasses that are now entering the market. It holds the camera at eye level, capturing roughly what I'm actually looking at. This is what preserves the implicit attention signal that's central to the design.

slides.subtitle: Design Iteration Log
slides.script:
Every change made during the calibration phase was logged here. Each entry records what was adjusted, why, and what effect it had.

This transparency was important: in a study where I'm both designer and subject, the log is the audit trail that keeps the process honest.

slides.subtitle: Autoethnographic Journal
slides.script:
And this is the journal interface — where I wrote my daily research observations alongside the agent's conversation transcripts.

The goal was to capture the texture of the experience: the moments where the agent anticipated something correctly, the moments where it missed completely, and the moments that surprised me.

slides.subtitle: Results
slides.script: Now — what did two weeks actually produce? Let's look at the data.

slides.subtitle: Full Timeline Wall (1/6)
slides.script:
This is the Timeline Wall — two weeks of my life, as seen by the agent. Each image is a moment the system judged worth capturing.

What strikes me every time I look at this is the sheer range: early mornings, late nights, working at my desk, cooking, going outside. The agent didn't curate this. It simply witnessed.

slides.subtitle: Activity Daily Rhythm Matrix
slides.script:
The Activity Rhythm Matrix maps what I was doing against the time of day, across the full two weeks.

What emerged wasn't random. There are clear bands — morning routines, deep work windows, evening patterns. What's interesting is how consistent they were, even on days that felt chaotic.

The agent can now recognize these rhythms — and adapt its support accordingly.

slides.subtitle: Object Co-occurrence Network
slides.script:
This network graph maps how objects appear together. Each node is an object; each connection means they appeared in the same scene.

The clusters reveal habits I didn't consciously know I had. My work setup always includes the same lamp, the same mug. My cooking context is completely separate. These aren't things I would have told an agent — but they're now part of how it understands me.

slides.subtitle: Context to Activity Flow
slides.script:
The Sankey diagram traces the flow between environments and activities. Where I was — desk, kitchen, couch — strongly predicted what I was doing next.

This confirms something intuitive: physical location is one of the most reliable signals for intent. If the agent knows where I am, it already has a strong guess about what I need.

slides.subtitle: Apartment Activity Heatmap
slides.script:
By projecting activities onto my floor plan, we can see where my life actually concentrates.

These hotspots aren't just coordinates. My desk is where I go to focus. My kitchen is where I go to decompress. The couch is where the in-between moments happen — the thinking, the reading, the brief breaks that never quite made it onto a calendar.

The agent now knows this.

slides.subtitle: Integrated Spatial Activity Map
slides.script:
This final map fuses movement with meaning — not just where I was, but what I was doing there, and how often.

What I find compelling about this image is what it would mean for someone who designs spaces. An architect or an interior designer doesn't just need to know how many square meters you have — they need to know how you actually inhabit a space. And right now, the only way to get that information is to ask you, and trust that you remember.

Imagine instead: they interview your agent. Yes, your agent. The system that has been quietly watching how you live for weeks, tracking where you focus, where you rest, where you feel at home.

That conversation — between a designer and an AI that genuinely knows its user — is closer than it sounds. And it's one of the futures this research is pointing toward.

slides.subtitle: What the Agent Learned About Me
slides.script:
So what does all this data actually become? These are real outputs from the agent's memory — things it learned about me over two weeks, not things I told it.

It noticed that my drink choices almost perfectly track what kind of work I'm doing. It recognized my late-night kitchen trips not as random movement, but as a consistent decompression loop. It saw that I always work with both physical paper and a screen at the same time.

These aren't things I would have thought to tell an agent. But now, it knows them.

slides.subtitle: Answering the Research Questions
slides.script:
The slide maps the key findings and limitations for each research question. I'll just highlight what surprised me most.

For RQ1: the system captures something digital logs fundamentally cannot — the in-between moments, the drift between tasks. But raw observation doesn't automatically become insight. That requires a dedicated reasoning step, and that's the part that still needs work.

For RQ2: the gap between the best and worst moments was stark. At its peak, the agent inferred I'd gone rock climbing without being told. At its worst, it told me I was cleaning my refrigerator coils while I sat at my desk.

The design requirements in RQ3 follow directly from those failures.

slides.subtitle: Moments of Connection & Disconnection
slides.script:
Let me close the analysis with two moments — one that worked, one that didn't.

The connection case: the agent noticed a gap in my log and asked if I'd gone rock climbing. It was right. That was the moment the system stopped feeling like a tool.

The disconnection case: I was sitting at my desk. The agent confidently told me I was cleaning the refrigerator coils.

The details are on the slide.

slides.subtitle: System Limitations
slides.script:
The slide lists four bottlenecks. A few things worth adding.

The Hawthorne effect was real — but what surprised me was how quickly I forgot about the camera when I was deeply focused. The social friction with third parties, on the other hand, was immediate and impossible to ignore.

And the VLM over-interpretation issue isn't just a bug. These models are built to find meaning. Give them a passive environment, and they'll invent it.

slides.subtitle: The Biographer Opens Its Eyes
slides.script:
This manga was generated by the agent itself — using the physical-world data it had collected about me over the two weeks.

I gave it no other brief. It already knew the story.

slides.subtitle: Thank You
slides.script: And with that, I'll conclude my presentation. Thank you very much for your time and attention. I am now open to any questions you may have.
